client: Lately, I’ve been feeling completely overwhelmed by my coursework in college. No matter how much I try, I feel like I’m falling behind, and it’s making me avoid my friends because I’m embarrassed and don’t want them to see me struggling. Honestly, I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like the problem is just me not being good enough to handle college.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy sense of disappointment in yourself, and the pressure to keep up is making you feel isolated. I wonder if we could explore together how much of this belief that you’re "not good enough" might be rooted in unhelpful self-critical thoughts rather than facts? Therapy can be a space to unpack those feelings and find ways to move forward.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I do feel disappointed, but isn't it reasonable to feel that way when I can't keep up with the workload? Everyone else seems to manage fine, and I'm here pulling all-nighters just to stay afloat. It doesn't feel like self-criticism when it's just... reality.
therapist: Your voice sounds heavier than your words when you talk about everyone else managing fine—there’s a real weight to how you’re carrying this comparison. What do you think might happen if you allowed yourself to question whether "everyone else" is truly doing as well as they appear? Sometimes what looks effortless from the outside is far more complicated up close.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I guess some people might be struggling too, but they're still getting better grades than me. Even if they're not perfect, at least they're passing their classes without crying in the library bathroom. I don't know how to stop feeling like I'm the only one who can't handle this.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding yourself to a standard where even small struggles feel like failure—especially when you compare yourself to others. What would it feel like to extend the same kindness to yourself that you might offer to a friend who was feeling this way? It’s okay to not have everything figured out right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I don’t know... it’s hard to imagine being kind to myself when I feel like I’m letting myself down. If I were a friend, I’d probably tell them it’s okay to take a break or ask for help, but when it’s me, it feels like I’m just making excuses or being lazy. I don’t want to cut myself slack if it means I’ll fall even further behind.
therapist: You’re holding yourself to such a strict standard—one where even self-compassion feels like a risk. I hear how much you fear that being kinder to yourself might mean giving up, when in reality, it could be what helps you find the strength to keep going. What do you think it would take to test that belief, even in a small way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe I could try being less hard on myself for one day—just one—and see if it helps. But honestly, I'm scared that if I let up even a little, I'll just completely stop trying. What if I test it and end up proving that I need to be this hard on myself to function?
therapist: It’s clear how much weight you’re carrying with this fear—that if you soften even a little, everything might fall apart. What if, instead of seeing self-compassion as letting go, we framed it as giving yourself the energy to keep moving forward? Testing it for one day doesn’t mean abandoning your responsibilities; it might just mean approaching them from a different mindset.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I could try framing it that way, but what if I still feel just as overwhelmed but now I’m also mad at myself for being “soft”? I’ve been so used to pushing myself hard that it feels weird to even consider being kind to myself. It’s like I don’t trust myself to handle things if I’m not being tough.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of uncertainty and even some fear about what might happen if you shift away from being so tough on yourself. That push-and-pull between wanting to try something new and worrying it won’t work is really understandable. How might it feel to experiment with small, manageable steps—like noticing when you’re being self-critical and gently questioning whether it’s truly helping?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I could try noticing when I’m being self-critical, but it’s hard because those thoughts feel so automatic—like they’re just part of who I am. I’m not sure if questioning them will really change anything, but I guess I’m willing to try if it means I might feel less overwhelmed eventually.
therapist: It’s brave of you to be open to trying something new, even when it feels unfamiliar or uncertain. Those self-critical thoughts can feel so ingrained, almost like they’re part of your identity, but noticing them is the first step to creating space for something different. What do you think might happen if you started to gently challenge those thoughts, even just once a day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if I challenged those thoughts, I might feel less like I’m drowning all the time. But it’s hard to imagine what I’d even say to myself—like, what’s the alternative to “I’m not good enough”? It feels fake or forced to try to tell myself something positive when I don’t really believe it yet.
therapist: It sounds like you’re grappling with how to shift those self-critical thoughts without feeling like you’re lying to yourself—and that’s a really valid concern. Maybe instead of trying to force positive statements, we could focus on neutral ones, like “I’m doing the best I can right now,” and see how that feels. What do you think about starting there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I think I could try saying something neutral like that, but it still feels a bit uncomfortable—like I’m avoiding the truth. What if I’m not actually doing the best I can? What if I’m just not trying hard enough and saying that is just letting myself off the hook?
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real tension between wanting to try a different approach and the fear that it might mean you’re not holding yourself accountable. That discomfort you’re feeling—it’s okay to sit with it. What if we explored what “trying hard enough” really means to you? Sometimes our standards for ourselves can be so much harsher than what we’d expect from anyone else.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don't know what "trying hard enough" really means—I just feel like if I'm not exhausted and miserable, then I must not be working hard enough. But when I say that out loud, it sounds kind of unhealthy. I guess I've never really thought about whether my standards are realistic or not.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to question whether tying your worth to exhaustion might be more harmful than helpful—that’s a really important realization. What do you think it would look like to redefine “trying hard enough” in a way that includes your well-being, not just your output?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
